entry.title: Connected by Design: Run Integrated Business Processes, Out of the Box
entry.content:
Running a business well depends on connected processes working together across the organization. A customer opportunity can flow seamlessly through to revenue recognition, a purchase request can move smoothly through to supplier payment, and a workforce plan can connect a hiring decision to a productive employee. Finance and human resources (HR) shape many of these outcomes, giving both functions a unique opportunity to turn connected processes and data into better decisions for the entire business.

 

The strategic question Finance and HR can answer together

Finance and HR often approach the same business opportunity from two complementary angles. Finance brings a cost and capacity lens: how licensing, integration, and infrastructure decisions translate into what the organization can actually execute on. HR brings a focus on agility and the ability to launch initiatives like a new onboarding cycle as the business requires. Bringing those perspectives together opens up a better question: What becomes possible when Finance and HR work from a real-time, intelligent view of the business?

Each system reflected the priorities, requirements, and possibilities of the moment in which it was selected. As the business evolved, those individual choices created an opportunity to bring together what had previously been managed separately. It's no longer a question of whether each system works on its own, but how Finance and HR can build on those investments to create a shared foundation for the decisions they increasingly need to make together.

 

When Finance and HR work from the same context

The organizations leading this shift tend to have one thing in common. They're organizing workforce strategy around a single source of insight rather than around separate functional perspectives. When those workflows connect, the data they produce isn't Finance's version and HR's version sitting side by side. It's one shared picture, built on the same definitions from the start. Connected workflows give Finance and HR the context to evaluate priorities, respond to change, and give leaders a stronger basis for timely, confident decisions.

That shared approach turns integration into everyday business value. Workforce planning becomes a continuous exchange between Finance and HR, while scenario modeling gives CFOs and CHROs something they can act on, not just present. Compliance becomes easier to manage, and smoother handoffs across hiring, onboarding, and budgeting help the organization move forward with greater speed and confidence.

The result is a different kind of conversation. Finance and HR can spend less time establishing context and more time evaluating options, setting priorities, and acting together. Alignment becomes the starting point rather than the outcome.

 

How SAP-managed public cloud ERP turns connection into business value

Across our customer conversations, one thing kept coming up: customers want to focus on business outcomes from day one, with the applications and integrations ready to support them.

SAP-managed public cloud ERP provides that foundation, connecting business processes and data so that teams can work efficiently across functions and turn shared insight into coordinated action. When a customer selects a business scenario like Workforce Management, the integration comes out of the box. SAP provisions all required applications and integration in one guided experience, keeping technical decisions to a minimum and taking care of monitoring and operations. Customers and partners implement the full scenario together, and partners go straight to business design and the outcomes that matter most to customers. Workforce Management (SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central) and Operational Procurement (SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP Ariba Buying and Invoicing) are both running in Early Adopter phase now. The next scenario is Opportunity to Order (SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP Sales Cloud V2).

The SAP-managed public cloud ERP community is where you can get the full picture on the latest scenarios, the Early Adopter Care program, as well as blog posts, webinars, and opportunities to learn from customers and partners making the same shift. Connect with us there to ask questions and explore how to get involved or find more under the tag "SAP-managed Public Cloud ERP". If this post sparked a question or an idea, continue the conversation in the comments.

entry.title: 2 Key Important updates in Position Management in H2 2026
entry.content:
1. Default for Moving Currently Assigned Position Under New Manager's Position

Before this release, if you changed an employee’s manager in job information the option to "Move Currently Assigned Position Below New Manager's Position" was displayed and defaulted to No.  In the H2 2026 release there is a new setting in the Position Management Settings which enables you to default this option to Yes. This is located in the UI Customizing tab:

NOTE: the option to "Move Currently Assigned Position Below New Manager's Position" is controlled through RBP – Manage Positions – Option to Move Position to New Manager in Job Info Change.  This feature only works if you have enabled the latest editing and history UI in Configure Latest People Profile – General Settings:

Below is a reminder about how this feature behaves.  If you update an employee’s manager in Job Information it will move the employee's position (and all lower level positions) to be under the new manager's position. In this example, Chloe sits under Arjita, both as an employee and a position.

If we process the change in manager in Job Information whether through ‘take action’ or via ‘Quick Actions’, the option "Move Currently Assigned Position Below New Manager's Position" will render and will be defaulted to Yes.

When this is marked as Yes then the following will occur:

  • Chloe is moved under William
  • Chloe’s position is moved under William’s position
  • Any positions under Chloe are moved with her position
  • A job information record is added based on the event reason derivation
 
 

 

 

 

  • Position Org Chart is updated

 

 
 

 

It is important to note, that if you delete the Job Information record this will not re-adjust the positions in the org chart.  You would need to go Manage Position and delete the time slice from the position as a separate action.

2. Triggering Reclassification When Moving Positions With a Manager Change

Before this release, if you made a change in Job Information through Manager Self-Service or an Employee Central Quick Action and changed the employee's manager and another position attribute field at the same time, the Position Reclassification was simply suppressed, potentially resulting in inconsistent data between Position and Job Information. For example if you updated manager and cost center, cost center would not be updated back to the position.  You would have to process the change as two separate transactions, or make the changes on the Position object only.

In H2 2026 release there is a new setting that allows you to make the updates in one transaction

 

In the example below Chloe new Manager is Will, and her cost center is changing at the same time.

The Position Org Chart relationship is updated:

And Chloe's position is updated to reflect the new cost center:

NOTE: In order for the reclassification to work, the Job Info to Position syncing rule must be configured and on the event reason the "Follow-Up Activity in Position" option must be set to "Position Reclassification.

What key benefits does this enhancement bring?

Previously, when an employee's manager changed without the employee moving into a new position, this update was best done by HR so they could ensure both position and job information updates remained in sync with each other. The process involved either managing all changes on the position object and let the changes sync to Job Information or make the changes in a two step process in Job Information. This put more work onto HR and there was a risk to data integrity if a step was missed.  

This latest enhancement provides an intuitive and consistent way for managers to process this kind of change for their direct reports, either through MSS-Take Action or through an Employee Central Quick Action.  The data is updated in a single step, thereby reducing the risk of data errors.

More information can be found on help.sap.com here:

Moving Positions When Changing the Manager | SAP Help Portal

 Triggering Reclassification When Moving Positions With a Manager Change | SAP Help Portal

entry.title: Must-Knows: Moving a Non-SAP Workforce to SuccessFactors in an M&A Engagement
entry.content:
Must-Knows: Moving a Non-SAP Workforce to SuccessFactors in an M&A Engagement

Lift and shift or harmonize? A high-level guide to the critical focus areas

 

Applies when the parent runs on SAP SuccessFactors and acquired company runs on a different HR platform like Workday.

Summary

When an acquired company runs on a non-SAP HCM platform and the parent runs on SAP SuccessFactors, the integration is rarely a single decision. It is a series of area-by-area choices between two paths: lift and shift the acquired company's way of working or harmonize onto the parent's standards.

Two ways to bring an acquired population into the parent system

LIFT AND SHIFT

HARMONIZE

•     Keep the acquired structures

•     Fastest path and lowest Day 1 risk (based upon TSA timeline)

•     Honors commitments to employees

•     Creates clean-up work after go-live

•     Adopt the parent's standards

•     Unified structure, cleaner analytics

•     Needs HR and business alignment

•     Higher change impact for employees on day 1

 

Part A: Foundation Areas

These areas define how people, jobs, and organizations are represented in SuccessFactors Employee Central.

1. Job Architecture

Job codes, job families, levels and grades, job profiles, titles

Lift and shift

Carry the acquired company's job codes and titles into SuccessFactors as-is, utilizing existing job families and adding new.

Harmonize

Map all acquired roles into the parent's existing job architecture before load.

Focus areas

•     Mapping Workday job profiles to EC job classifications

•     Preserving FLSA/exempt status and EEO and other compliance fields

•     Level calibration, pay range impact, and title changes if harmonizing

•     Impact on compa-ratio for compensation module

Best practice

Lift and shift for Day 1 so harmonization can happen later without rework, unless the role mapping is obvious and already approved.

 

2. Organization Structure and Legal Entities

Supervisory orgs vs. departments, cost centers, legal entities, positions

Lift and shift

Recreate the acquired structure as a standalone branch in the parent's org tree.

Harmonize

Fold teams into the parent's departments, cost centers, and reporting lines.

Focus areas

•     Legal entity and cost center setup (finance and payroll dependencies)

•     Position management vs. non-position models

•     Manager hierarchy accuracy and approval chains (OrgLab can be used to define future state reporting structure)

•     Employees with dotted-line or matrix relationships

Best practice

Keep a clear structure as much as possible at go-live, then you can align in planned waves based upon finance and legal entity decisions.

 

3. Compensation and Benefits Structures

Pay grades, salary ranges, bonus plans, benefit plans, merit cycles

Lift and shift

Preserve existing pay structures and plan eligibility to honor commitments.

Harmonize

Move employees to the parent's structures and programs.

Focus areas

•     There may be Legal or contractual obligations to maintain pay and benefits for a defined period

•     Country-specific compensation plans

•     Integration with payroll and benefits vendors

•     Alignment of merit and bonus cycles with the go-live

Best practice

Cover the existing terms at transition. Harmonization can be done later with job architecture harmonization

 

4. Business Rules and Workflows

Approvals, hire/term/transfer rules,event reasons

Lift and shift

Replicate acquired company processes in SuccessFactors as closely as possible.

Harmonize

Adopt the parent's standard workflows and rules.

Focus areas

•     Workday business processes do not map one-to-one to SF workflows and business rules

•     Defaults such as work schedule hours at hire

•     Termination logic and workflow conditions

•     Event and reason code alignment

Best practice

Default to the parent's standard processes. Replicating acquired company logic in SF usually adds complexity at go-live. Make exceptions only for legal or country needs for a successful go-live

 

5. Security and Access (RBP)

Role-based permissions, groups, sensitive data, single sign-on

Lift and shift

Replicate the acquired company's security roles.

Harmonize

Build access on the parent's role and group model.

Focus areas

•     Rebuild in RBP groups and roles rather than copying Workday/third party security to avoid continuing security policies that were not effective

•     Target population groups for the acquired company

•     Country-based restrictions

•     Tighter controls sensitive data such as dependents, national IDs

Best practice

Always harmonize. Replicating another platform's security model is not recommended

 

6. Country Configuration and Compliance

New countries, statutory fields, data privacy, regulatory reporting

Lift and shift

Configure acquired countries as stand-alone setups with their own picklists, fields, and templates.

Harmonize

Align to the parent's country configurations where they already exist.

Focus areas

•     Statutory fields and local labor law requirements

•     New country setup where the parent has no footprint

•     Document and contract templates by country

•     Regulatory reporting continuity (for example EEO and VETS-4212 in the US)

•     Data privacy requirements such as GDPR

Best practice

Build a country-by-country readiness checklist with local HR and Legal sign-off. Reuse the parent's configuration where it exists and add only the gaps.

 

7. Historical Data

Effective-dated history, archives, retention, right of access

Lift and shift

Load as much history as the data model allows.

Harmonize

Load current state record into SuccessFactors

Focus areas

•     Full history should not be converted

•     Retention policy and who can access the archive after transition

•     GDPR right of access

•     Former employees' future needs: tax, immigration, benefits, legal matters

Best practice

This is often underestimated and surfaces late, usually when a former employee or auditor asks for records that no longer exist in the new system. Define the retention and access model early: where history lives, who can access it, and how former employees can request their records.

 

Part B: Talent Modules

8. Performance and Goals Management (PMGM)

Goals, review cycles, ratings, calibration, feedback, development plans

Performance touches pay, promotion, and how employees feel about being evaluated by a new company. It is also closely scrutinized by works councils.

 

Lift and shift

Build separate templates, rating scales, and cycle dates in SF for the acquired population.

Harmonize

Assign acquired employees to the parent's existing forms, scale, and calendar.

Focus areas

•     Template and permission assignment by population

•     Rating scale crosswalk (for example 5-point to 4-point or 5-point to 5-point) – determine how past ratings map

•     Route maps and calibration sessions that include the new group

•     RBP visibility for ratings and feedback

•     Performance history of employees

•     Complete in flight cycle in legacy system

Best Practice

Honor the in-flight cycle through completion, then onboard the acquired population into the parent's process at the start of the next cycle. Build a rating scale crosswalk and archive historical ratings with controlled access. In Scenario B, skip building a temporary SF process if the parent will not use that module.

9. Recruitment and Talent Acquisition

Requisitions, candidates, offers, onboarding handoff, compliance reporting

Hiring does not pause on go-live day. Open requisitions, in-flight candidates, and offers must continue, and offers are legally sensitive.

 

Lift and shift

Create separate requisition templates, approval flows, and offer letter templates for the acquired population.

Harmonize

Use the parent's templates, workflows, and career site.

Focus areas

•     Requisition and offer approval workflows

•     Requisition templates tied to job architecture

•     Onboarding handoff to EC and country-specific fields

Best Practice

Harmonize while protecting in-flight offers.

 

10. Learning

Catalog, curricula, assignments, transcripts, compliance training

Lift and shift

Migrate the acquired company's courses, curricula, and assignments.

Harmonize

Move the acquired population into the parent's catalog and assignment model.

Focus areas

•     Completion records and certifications that are compliance-critical

•     Assignment profiles and exclusion rules, so parent-company mandatory assignments do not flood the acquired population unintentionally

•     Content licensing

•     Access for employees and managers

Best practice

Migrate completion records for compliance-critical items only. Use exclusion rules to control assignments, then phase the acquired population into the parent catalog on a planned schedule.

 

Part C: Operations and Experience

These areas keep people paid, informed, and productive from the first day on the new platform.

11. Time Off and Work Schedules

Leave policies, accruals, balances, holiday calendars, default hours

Lift and shift

Recreate the acquired policies and accrual rules, and carry over balances.

Harmonize

Move to the parent's policies.

Focus areas

•     Policy gaps in countries where the parent has no equivalent (manual tracking or a vendor solution)

•     Work schedule defaults, such as hours defaulting at new hire

•     Configure work schedules for time off calculations

•     Holiday calendars by location

Best practice

Lift and shift at go-live. Changing leave policies mid-transition can create issues. Flag country gaps early and decide on manual or vendor tracking.

 

12. Employee Experience and Language Support

Self-service, mobile, documents, language, help desk, communications

Lift and shift

Provide a separate portal or landing experience for the acquired population.

Harmonize

Move employees to the parent's portal, mobile app, and support model.

Focus areas

•     Employee and manager self-service readiness

•     Language support gaps in the UI and translated job aids

•     Help desk and case routing for the new population

•     Communications and training before and after cutover

Best practice

Use the parent's company experience, and close language gaps before go-live. Translated materials also support the works council conversation.

entry.title: Works Council Engagement: The Make-or-Break Step in M&A HR (HCM) System Migrations
entry.content:
HR TECHNOLOGY M&A INTEGRATION

Works Council Engagement: The Make-or-Break Step in M&A HR System Migrations

Co-determination, consultation, and approval rights over HR systems and employee data

 

Who this is for: program leads, HRIS teams, Legal, and Privacy teams moving an acquired workforce onto a new HR platform (for example from Workday into SAP SuccessFactors) where acquired employees sit in countries with works councils.

1. Why this is a gating item?

Works council engagement is not a lift and shift vs. harmonize choice. In countries with works councils, the council often has legal rights to be informed, consulted, or to approve a new HR system before employee data can move. Missing this can delay go-live regardless of how ready the technology is.

The core message

A system can be fully configured, tested, and signed off by the business, and still be blocked at the last step. Treat works council approval as a formal go-live readiness criteria, owned and tracked like any other critical path item.

 

2. Understand the rights you are dealing with

The spectrum of works council rights

INFORM

→

CONSULT

→

CONSENT

Council receives the facts

before decisions are final

 

Council gives an opinion

and the employer must hear it

before deciding

 

No lawful rollout without

agreement, or a substitute

ruling or conciliation

Rights differ by country and by what the system does. Always confirm with local counsel.

Why HR systems usually trigger these rights?

  • An HR platform holds personnel data, and rules about processing and protecting that data are often subject to council rights.
  • Several statutes look at capability, not intent. A system that can observe or record behavior or performance can trigger consent rights even if the employer promises not to use it that way.
  • Talent modules go further. Performance, goals, and assessment criteria are frequently treated as evaluation schemes, which have their own consent or consultation rules.
  • Analytics, dashboards, and AI-assisted features can widen the scope. Switching a feature on later can reopen the discussion.

How the level shapes your plan?

Level

What it means for the program

Plan for

Inform

No veto, but early notice builds trust and avoids disputes later

•     Brief the council early

•     Share a dossier summary and a named contact

Consult

The council's opinion must be heard before the decision is taken, so timing matters

•     Allow a real review period

•     Document how feedback was handled

•     Decide only after consultation closes

Consent

The council can withhold agreement, which may lead to negotiation, conciliation, or a court route

•     Treat as critical path

•     Negotiate a written agreement

•     Prepare a contingency per country

 

3. What works councils typically focus on?

Councils generally ask the same core questions, even when the legal basis differs. Preparing a clear answer to each, in writing and in the local language, is the single most effective way to shorten the process.

Topic

What the council asks

What should be done

Data

What employee data is collected, what moves to the new system, and why it is needed

•     Field-level data inventory: field, source, target, purpose

•     Rationale for each category, and what is not migrated

Data security

Where data is hosted, how it is protected, and who else can touch it

•     Hosting location, encryption, cross-border transfer mechanism

•     Vendor and sub-processor list with access scope

Data access

Who can see what, and how sensitive fields are protected

•     Role and permission matrix (managers, HR)

•     Live demo of what each role sees, including sensitive fields

Historical data

What is retained, what is archived, and how people can reach their records

•     Retention schedule and archive location

•     Process for current and former employees to request records

Monitoring

Assurance that the system will not be used to watch individuals

•     Written statement of purposes and prohibited uses

•     Status of analytics and AI features (on, off, planned)

Language

Whether employees can understand and use the system

•     Translated job aids, notices, and training

•     Known language gaps and the mitigation

Employee rights

How access, correction, and deletion requests are handled

•     GDPR rights process and contacts

•     Employee notice and communication plan

 

Tip: share the data model, not the data

The inventory should describe data elements and purposes, not individual employee records. Disclosing personal data to the council can itself need a legal basis, so keep examples anonymized or in test data.

 

4. A practical engagement approach

Run the works council track as its own workstream with an owner, a plan, and a status line in the program dashboard. A five-phase approach keeps Legal, Privacy, HR, and the program team aligned.

Five phases of works council engagement

1  Scope

2  Prepare

3  Brief and demo

4  Agree

5  Sustain

•     Identify entities and countries

•     Confirm council exists and level (local or central)

•     Agree owners and timeline

•     Align Legal, Privacy, HR on one answer set

•     Translate key materials

•     Early briefing, before design is final

•     Live demos of security and access

•     Log questions and commitments

•     Negotiate works agreement or opinion

•     Resolve open points in writing

•     Obtain formal approval or consultation close

•     Track as go-live criteria

•     Re-open if scope changes

•     Keep a named contact post go-live

 

Best practices:

  • Engage early, before design is final. Councils want to shape decisions, not rubber-stamp them.
  • If time permits bring critical employee level attributes inventory showing what is migrated and why.
  • Run live demos of the actual security model, role access, and what managers can see.
  • Be consistent with all countries works council: Align Legal, Privacy, and local HR, and document commitments in a works agreement where required.
  • Plan for their cycle. Build review cycles (weeks to months) into the plan, provide translated materials and a named contact, and track approval as a formal go-live readiness criteria.

entry.title: What I Learned Moving an Acquired Workforce (M&A) from Workday to SuccessFactors: 12 Lessons
entry.content:
What I Learned Moving an Acquired Workforce from Workday to SuccessFactors: 12 Lessons

What to plan for when moving an acquired company's employees onto a new HR system

Moving an acquired company's employees to a new HR system sounds simple: copy the data and hit a deadline. In practice, the system is often the easy part. The hard parts are outside vendors, agreements with acquired company, other projects going live at the same time, and things people assumed but never checked.

This lists twelve areas to plan for. They come from my experience moving an acquired workforce from Workday to SAP SuccessFactors.

At a glance

#

Area

What can go wrong

What to do?

1

Different vendors

The acquired company uses other payroll, time, and benefits providers.

Identify and decide who moves to the parent's vendors and who stays. If parent company selects new vendors let's say for time tracking for some countries then do plan in advance and align with the vendors.

2

Data Conversions

Mapping data from the acquired company’s HCM system to the parent company’s HCM system can be tricky. If data discussions are delayed, the impact reaches the whole project.

Start the mapping exercise early with the acquired company’s data team. Prioritize the critical path and the countries with most of the population. For low-headcount countries (e.g., under 20 employees), use workarounds and plan the final solution post go-live

3

Acquired Company agreement (TSA - Transition Services Agreement )

The acquired company may still run some services, so acquired company employees must not go to new vendors yet but will use existing services from legacy vendor.

In Integrations, add a filter by employee group and test it to ensure right employee population flows to the vendors.

4

Acquired company HCM system Logins

If accounts are made after the production employee data load,  the conveyed employees (acquired company employees) cannot get in on day one.

Usually accounts are activated and business email is created when employees are added to the system. In M&A projects, IT should plan this ahead in time so conveyed employees are able to login on day one.

5

Software updates

The software vendor updates, e.g. SuccessFactors - twice a year can change what you tested.

Updates should be reviewed and tested on priority

6

Parent Company Other Projects

The parent company may switch other tools on the go-live date or may have other internal HCM projects planned.

List the overlaps. Agree what comes first. Create a critical path based upon priorities.

7

Business keeps moving

Hires and changes continue during the move.

Set a freeze period for all HCM processes in parent and acquired company systems

8

Year-end timing

If it's a January go-live, it usually clashes with payroll year-end and holidays.

Check who is available. Plan extra support over the holidays.

9

Languages

The parent's system and documents may lack the acquired company's languages.

Check language support early. Translate legal items first. Plan job aid translations and system translations accordingly.

10

Training

Training is the first thing cut when time is short.

Train managers first. Keep it short and by role.

11

New countries and policies

The parent may never have set up some of the countries.

Use a checklist for each country, work with Legal and plan to keep it simple as critical path for go-live.

12

Approvals and alignment with legal and works council

Legal approvals and work council approvals are critical

Treat approvals as must-haves.

 

PART 1

Vendors and connections

1   Different vendors

In short: The acquired company rarely uses the same vendors as the parent.

  • Payroll. This is the most sensitive area. Decide early whether employees move to the parent's payroll provider on day one, stay with their current one, or move country by country. Staying is often safest for the first pay runs, but it means building and testing an extra connection.
  • Time tracking. Hours worked drive pay. If shift rules or extra pay rates do not match, pay will be wrong.
  • Vendor availability. Each extra vendor is a team you do not control hence plan properly.
  • Vendor setup. Security checks and access approvals can take longer than the build itself.

2   Data Conversions

In short: Accurate data is essential: every HCM process and downstream system depends on it working correctly

  • The two systems are built around different org structures, job architectures, codes and business rules, so most data cannot simply be copied across. Each element needs a mapping decision, and those decisions often need input from HR, business and legal owners on both sides.
  • Work closely with the IT, and other workstreams that are dependent on the HCM data you are converting to avoid gaps and stay on track.

3   The acquired company agreement decides who goes where

In short: A Transition Services Agreement (TSA) means the acquired company keeps providing some services, such as payroll or benefits, for a set time.

  • Use a filter. A simple rule, such as a flag, decides which employees are sent to which vendor, and when that changes.
  • Test both ways. Add the filter to every connection. Check who is sent and who is not.
  • Plan the end. When the TSA ends, the filter is removed. Treat that as its own go-live.

Without this, someone may be paid twice, not paid at all, or sent to a vendor they should not be in.

4   Logins must be ready before go-live

In short: People cannot log in if their accounts do not exist yet.

  • Create accounts early. If access depends on the company's login system, such as Active Directory or single sign-on, accounts may not exist when the data arrives. Create them before the data load.
  • Know the login method. Whether people sign in with the company login or a password decides who fixes lockouts and resets.
  • Test as a real employee. Try the first login the way an employee would, not as an administrator.
  • Agree on names. Settle usernames, email formats, number ranges for objects and employees, and whether employee IDs stay the same.

PART 2

Timing and change

5   Software updates follow their own calendar

In short: Updates can change features you already tested.

Cloud software like SuccessFactors gets major updates twice a year, and the dates will not match your project plan. On this project, an update affected the performance module for which the fix from SAP was planned on date which was late for the project so feature was disabled and we had to go with an old version of the performance template.

  • Put update dates on the project calendar from the start.
  • Re-test what already worked after each update.
  • Give one person the job of reading the release notes.

6   Other projects at the parent go live too

In short: Your go-live date is rarely the only change.

The parent company may switch other tools on the same date, for example moving the employee help desk from Employee Central Service Center to ServiceNow, or changing a payroll provider.

  • List the overlaps. Find where the other projects touch yours, such as ticket types, workflows, connections, and links employees use.
  • Decide what comes first. If one change slips, agree which has priority and who decides.
  • Prepare support. Make sure acquired employees know where to send requests on day one, with help articles and trained agents.
  • Share one calendar. Everyone should see freeze periods, test dates, and announcements from other projects.
  • Watch shared people. The same experts, testers, and approvers are often needed by both projects.

7   The business does not stop during the move

In short: Hires, exits, promotions, and team changes keep happening.

  • Set a freeze. Stop changes in the old system for a short time, and decide how to handle changes made during it.
  • Plan a final load. Catch changes made after the last data copy.
  • Watch recent changes. Promotions, transfers, and pay changes with dates close to go-live are easy to miss.
  • Name an owner. Decide who enters anything that falls through by hand.

8   Go-live often lands on year-end

In short: A January 1 go-live collides with payroll year-end, tax reports, and holidays.

  • Check people's availability over the go-live weekend and the days after.
  • Check vendor freezes. Many vendors stop changes around year-end.
  • Plan extra support around holiday cover, not the usual work calendar.

PART 3

People and experience

9   Languages: the acquired company may have more than the parent

In short: The parent's system and documents may not cover every language the acquired company uses.

  • Check language support in screens, forms, and notices for every country. Gaps tend to show up late.
  • Translate the important items first: privacy notices, offer letters, policies, and how-to guides.
  • Have a native speaker review translations, especially legal wording.
  • Remember works councils often ask for translated materials before they can review.

10   Training gets squeezed

In short: Training is usually the first thing cut, yet employees and managers must work in the new system.

  • Train managers first. They answer most questions and run processes like performance and onboarding.
  • Keep it short. Quick guides, short videos, and live walk-throughs beat long courses.
  • Time it well. Training too early is forgotten, and too late does not help.
  • Cover all time zones and languages, and record sessions for people who cannot attend.
  • Offer extra support after go-live. Daily open sessions in the first weeks catch what training missed.

11   New countries, policies, and default settings

In short: The acquired company may have employees in countries the parent has never set up.

  • New country setup needs local fields, templates, and legal checks.
  • Policy gaps are common, such as a time-off policy for a country where the parent has none. That can mean tracking by hand or buying a tool.
  • Default settings can quietly cause errors, such as working hours for new hires or end-of-employment steps.
  • Systems do not match one-to-one. Understand the idea first, then match the fields.

PART 4

Control and quality

12   Works Council and Legal approvals 

In short: Some of the most important items are not technical.

  • Works councils. In countries such as Germany, an employee representative body may need to be informed, consulted, or give approval before employee data moves. Treat approval as a must-have for go-live and start well in advance.
  • Offer letters and contract templates. They need legal review for the new employer and local law. If the hiring tool's build waits on that review, so does its testing so this should be planned well in advance and tracked throughout the implementation of project

entry.title: Identity Propagation from Joule to SAP SuccessFactors
entry.content:
During workforce management reviews, HR managers and administrators frequently need to audit employee contract extension data. Searching through nested SAP SuccessFactors menus or manually parsing custom Metadata Framework (MDF) objects introduces friction into routine operations.

By integrating Joule with custom extension agents on SAP BTP, users can query sensitive custom MDF objects—such as Contract Renewal entities—using natural language while dynamically enforcing SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP) for every tool call.

Scenario Overview

  • Intent Initiation via Digital Assistant: An HR administrator or standard employee queries Joule using natural language to retrieve or verify contract renewal cases for an employee.
  • Identity Propagation & Session Context: Joule interprets the prompt and executes user identity propagation (principal propagation) down to SAP SuccessFactors, ensuring that the authenticated user's session context is preserved end-to-end.
  • Context-Aware RBP Enforcement: The custom agent fetches data directly from SuccessFactors OData APIs. Access to sensitive fields (such as salary adjustments or contract terms) is governed entirely by the user's assigned SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions.

This article walks through the end-to-end configuration: setting up trust between Joule and SuccessFactors, enabling principal propagation, and enforcing role-based access to the custom Contract Renewal MDF object.

Prerequisites

To successfully implement this architecture, ensure that the following system dependencies and administrative privileges are in place:

  • SAP BTP Subaccount with Joule Enabled: An active subaccount on SAP BTP with the Joule digital assistant entitlement subscribed and provisioned.
  • SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS): An IAS tenant configured as the Identity Provider for both your SAP BTP subaccount and your SAP SuccessFactors instance to enable OpenID Connect (OIDC) and SAML token exchanges.
  • Custom MDF Object in SuccessFactors: A custom Metadata Framework (MDF) object—such as Contract Renewal—created via Configure Object Definitions in SuccessFactors.
  • Role-Based Permissions (RBP) Configured: Specific permissions assigned in SuccessFactors RBP for the custom MDF object (e.g., read/write access granted to HR Manager, and restricted for Standard User).
  • Administrative Access: Administrator privileges across the SAP BTP Cockpit, the SAP IAS Administration Console, and the SuccessFactors Admin Center.
  • Protocol Familiarity: Basic understanding of OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect (OIDC), JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SAML 2.0 bearer assertions.

Architecture Overview

The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end trust chain and identity flow between Joule, SAP BTP, SAP Cloud Identity Services, and SAP SuccessFactors:
 
The identity flow begins when a user authenticates in Joule via SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS). Joule’s A2A client routes the prompt through a BTP Destination to the pro-code custom agent on SAP Cloud Foundry. The agent validates and forwards the user token, using a second BTP Destination to execute a SAML Bearer Assertion against SAP SuccessFactors. This ensures the request hits the OData API Center with the user's active session context, dynamically enforcing Role-Based Permissions (RBP) at the backend metadata layer.
 

Generate the SAML Signing Certificate

The BTP Destination Service will sign SAML assertions using a certificate. SuccessFactors needs that certificate registered to trust those assertions. Two commands are needed here because the outputs serve two different purposes and go to two different systems.

The first command generates the raw key material in PEM format — certificate.pem  is the public certificate you upload to SuccessFactors, and privateKey.pem is the private key that stays on your machine.

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout certs/privateKey.pem \
  -out certs/certificate.pem \
  -subj "/CN=sfsf-assistant-saml"

The second command takes those two PEM files and bundles them together into a PKCS#12 keystore (.p12). This is the format BTP Destination Service expects when it needs to sign SAML assertions on behalf of your application — a plain PEM file is not sufficient for this purpose.

openssl pkcs12 -export \
  -in certs/certificate.pem \
  -inkey certs/privateKey.pem \
  -out certs/sfsf-saml-client.p12 \
  -name "sfsf-saml-client" \
  -password pass:yourpassword

certificate.pem goes to SuccessFactors when registering the OAuth2 client. sfsf-saml-client.p12 goes to the BTP Destination Service certificate store. Remember, the password for your .p12 certificate will be required when you use it in the destination configuration. 

Register an OAuth2 Client in SuccessFactors

SuccessFactors needs to know your app's signing certificate before it will accept SAML assertions from it.

1. Log in to SuccessFactors Admin Center. Navigate to Admin Center → Manage OAuth2 Client Applications or Under the tools Search field type Manage OAuth2 Client Applications and click the link in the search results.

2. Click Register Client Application

3. When you click Register Client Application under Manage OAuth2 Client Applications in SAP SuccessFactors, you will need to fill out the following form fields:

  • Company: Pre-filled automatically based on your current SuccessFactors instance or tenant ID.
  • Application Name: A unique, descriptive name for your client application or integration.
  • Description (Optional): A short note explaining the purpose of the application or integration.
  • Application URL: A valid URL pointing to the client application or vendor's website domain.
  • X.509 Certificate: Paste your pre-generated public certificate text which we generated in the previous section.

and click Register

4. After clicking Register, the system generates a public API Key required for authenticating your API requests. To retrieve this key, locate your new client entry in the list, navigate to the Actions column, and click View.

5.Locate the generated API Key. Copy it and store it safely, as your external application will require it to complete the connection.

Maintain the Generated Certificate in BTP Destination Service

Before configuring the destination itself, the .p12 keystore must be uploaded to the BTP Destination Service certificate store. The destination references it by name — it is never embedded inline.

1. Login into the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to your Subaccount. Go to Connectivity and navigate directly to Destination Certificates and click on Import Button.

2. Click the Upload button to select your certificate file from your local file system

3. Select sfsf-saml-client.p12  from your local machine and click on Open button.

4. Click on Create button

Once uploaded, the certificate appears in the list with the name sfsf-saml-client.p12. This is the exact value you will enter as Key Store Location when configuring the sfsf-conn destination.

The certificate store is scoped to your BTP subaccount. Multiple destinations in the same subaccount can reference the same uploaded keystore.

Import the Destinations

With the certificate uploaded, you can now create the destination that performs the actual principal propagation. This destination is what your application calls to exchange the user's IAS token for a SuccessFactors OAuth token.
Rather than filling in every property manually, download the pre-built destination file below and import it directly into BTP. You only need to update the four placeholder values specific to your SuccessFactors tenant before importing.

Download: (destinations/sfsf-conn.properties)

Open the file and replace the following placeholders with your own values:

Authentication=OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
KeyStoreLocation=sfsf-saml-client.p12
KeyStorePassword=<keystore-password>
Name=sfsf-conn
ProxyType=Internet
SAMLAssertionProvider=DestinationServiceGenerated
Type=HTTP
URL=<successfactors-api-url>
apiKey=<generated-api-key-in-successfactor>
audience=www.successfactors.com
authnContextClassRef=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PreviousSession
clientKey=<generated-api-key-in-successfactor>
companyId=<company-id-in-successfactor>
includeSigningCertificateInSAMLAssertion=true
nameIdFormat=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:unspecified
skipUserAttributesPrefixInSAMLAttributes=true
skipUserUuidInSAMLAttributes=true
tokenServiceURL=<successfactors-api-url>/oauth/token
tokenServiceURLType=Dedicated
  • <successfactors-api-url>:  SAP  API domain (e.g., api12sales.successfactors.eu) — appears in both URL and tokenServiceURL
  • <generated-api-key-in-successfactor>: The API Key (Client ID) generated during OAuth2 registration in SF — appears in both clientKey and apiKey.
  • <company-id-in-successfactor>:  Your SAP SF company/tenant ID.
  • <keystore-password>:  The password set for the uploaded .p12 X.509 certificate used for SAML signing.

All other properties — authentication type, SAML settings, certificate flags — are already correctly configured in the file. Once you have updated the placeholders, import the file into BTP:

1. Go to BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations then click Create.

2. In the Create New Destination dialog box, select From File to import an already configured destination.

Principal Propagation from Joule to Agent

With Joule’s Pro-Code Extensibility, customers can seamlessly integrate custom, code-based agents into the Joule ecosystem using third-party frameworks—a paradigm known as "Bring Your Own Agent" (BYOA). Rather than relying solely on declarative Joule frameworks, a BYOA agent operates as a standard, code-based application that communicates directly with Joule via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. However, extending Joule’s capabilities with custom logic requires careful consideration of how enterprise data is accessed.

For any production-grade agent interacting with core enterprise platforms like SAP SuccessFactors, implementing Principal Propagation (User Identity Propagation) is non-negotiable. Omitting identity propagation forces the agent to execute requests under a generic technical user identity, which inherently bypasses individual Role-Based Permissions (RBP) and exposes the organization to major architectural, security, and governance risks.

With principal propagation active, data authorization is enforced directly at the backend source system layer in SuccessFactors. This guarantees that unauthorized data payloads are stopped at the source and never exposed to intermediate agent layers or the client application — making identity propagation the core mechanism for maintaining strict enterprise compliance.

Achieving this level of security requires building a continuous chain of trust across the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP). The previous steps established the connection between SAP SuccessFactors and the BTP environment to enable user-propagated API calls. The next phase establishes trust between Joule and the agent. The resulting end-to-end authentication pipeline flows from the Joule-managed SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS) tenant, through the agent, and directly into SAP SuccessFactors — yielding a stateless, credential-less agent that holds no long-lived backend credentials, ensuring every backend request is executed strictly within the real-time permissions of the logged-in user.

The setup for establishing trust between Joule and the agent follows the foundation outlined by Felix Bartler in his article, Joule A2A: Propagate the User Identity from Joule into S/4HANA. You may follow the steps directly from Felix's guide or proceed with the tailored implementation steps outlined below.

Registering the IAS Applications for App-to-App Trust

IAS acts as the gatekeeper for every token exchange in this chain. Before Joule can hand its token to your agent, IAS needs to know who each participant is and needs explicit authorization for each step in the exchange. That means registering two OpenID Connect applications — one representing the proxy, one representing your agent — and then drawing the permission path between them.

Both applications must be created in the same IAS tenant where your BTP subaccount established trust during Joule provisioning. You can confirm which tenant that is under Subaccount → Security → Trust Configuration.

Create the IAS Applications

In the IAS admin panel, navigate to Applications & Resources → Applications and create two OpenID Connect applications:

1. A2A_Proxy_App — the intermediary that receives Joule's token and hands it forward. After creating it, expose an API resource on the application (e.g., a2a_proxy_app_api). This API defines the audience (aud) claim that exchanged tokens will carry, which IAS uses to validate that the exchange is directed at the right target.

2. A2A_Custom_Agent_Apps — the application representing your actual agent, the one that will call SuccessFactors. Expose an API resource here as well (e.g., a2a_custom_agent_app_api), for the same reason.

Configure the Trust Chain

Dependencies in IAS define which token exchanges are permitted. In this setup, you need to configure two specific application dependencies: the inbound Joule proxy dependency and the downstream target application dependency.

1. Joule → Proxy: Locate the pre-existing Joule IAS application in your tenant. Add a dependency targeting A2A_Proxy_App  and select its exposed API. Name this dependency exactly joule-to-proxy — this string is hardcoded into Joule's runtime and cannot be changed.

2. Proxy → Agent: Open A2A_Proxy_App and add a dependency targeting  A2A_Custom_Agent_App. Name it proxy-to-target. This name is your choice, but you will need to reference it exactly in the BTP Destination configuration in the next section.

Because the joule-to-proxy dependency is fixed to your proxy app once, adding a future agent requires only a new IAS application and a new proxy-to-<name> dependency on the same proxy — no changes to Joule's configuration.

Finally, generate a client secret on A2A_Proxy_App under Client Authentication → Secrets. The BTP Destination Service will use these credentials to authenticate as the proxy when performing the second token exchange. Save the client ID and secret — you will need them in the next section.

Key Implementation Patterns

Three core components in the agent application work together to pass the user's identity from the inbound A2A request all the way into SAP SuccessFactors. The agent logic itself (agent.py) remains completely decoupled from security tokens, while two supporting layers handle identity capture and downstream token exchange.

1. Inbound Identity Capture (main.py)

A Starlette middleware intercepts inbound A2A requests, extracts the bearer token, and validates it against your IAS tenant before storing it in the request context:

class IASAuthMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        auth = request.headers.get("authorization", "")
        token = auth.removeprefix("Bearer ").strip() if auth.startswith("Bearer ") else None

        if token and (claims := _verify_ias_token(token)):
            set_user_token(token)  # Store token in context for active request thread

        return await call_next(request)

During local development, setting IAS_ISSUER and IAS_AUDIENCE to local placeholders bypasses token signature checks so you can test using mock tokens without modifying code.

2. Downstream Token Exchange (sfsf_client.py)

When tools fetch data from SuccessFactors, sfsf_client.py retrieves the context token and passes it to the SAP BTP Destination Service via the X-user-token header:

def get_sfsf_token_and_url() -> tuple[str, str]:
    creds = _get_dest_service_creds()
    user_token = get_user_token()

    # Get Destination Service access token
    ds_token = httpx.post(
        f"{creds['url']}/oauth/token",
        data={"grant_type": "client_credentials"},
        auth=(creds["clientid"], creds["clientsecret"]),
    ).json()["access_token"]

    # Request SuccessFactors token with user identity attached
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {ds_token}"}
    if user_token:
        headers["X-user-token"] = user_token  # Triggers SAML assertion for end-user

    dest = httpx.get(
        f"{creds['uri']}/destination-configuration/v1/destinations/sfsf-conn",
        headers=headers,
    ).json()

    return dest["authTokens"][0]["value"], dest["destinationConfiguration"]["URL"].rstrip("/")

Why X-user-token matters: Supplying the X-user-token header instructs the Destination Service to generate a user-bound SAML assertion. If omitted, the service falls back to the technical user configured on the destination, bypassing SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP).

Agent Tool Decoupling (agent.py)

Because the middleware and HTTP client manage identity propagation transparently, tools invoke standard OData calls directly:

@tool
def get_contract_renewal_cases(
    employee_id: str | None = None,
    status: str | None = None,
    department: str | None = None,
    faculty: str | None = None,
    top: int = 5,
) -> dict:
    """Fetch contract renewal cases from SuccessFactors.

    Use this tool to look up employment contract renewals, renewal dates, salary
    adjustments, performance grades, approval/review workflow status, and case notes
    for employees. Also covers vendor agreements and internal service transfers.

    Args:
        employee_id: Filter by employee userId (e.g. '103266'). Use userId, not username — resolve via search_employees first if needed.
        status:      Filter by case status (e.g. 'READY_FOR_SS_REVIEW', 'SS_REVIEWED_APPROVED', 'HRP_VALIDATED')
        department:  Filter by department code (e.g. 'ME')
        faculty:     Filter by faculty code (e.g. 'FoE')
        top:         Maximum number of results to return (default 5)
    """
    filters = []
    if employee_id:
        filters.append(f"cust_Employee eq '{employee_id}'")
    if status:
        filters.append(f"cust_status eq '{status}'")
    if department:
        filters.append(f"cust_department eq '{department}'")
    if faculty:
        filters.append(f"cust_faculty eq '{faculty}'")

    params = {
        "$select": (
            "externalCode,externalName,cust_Employee,cust_department,cust_faculty,"
            "cust_designation,cust_currentSalary,cust_newSalary,cust_salaryAdjustment,"
            "cust_performanceGrade,cust_currentEndDate,cust_proposedEndDate,"
            "cust_durationMonths,cust_discussionDate,cust_status,cust_notes,"
            "lastModifiedDateTime,lastModifiedBy,createdDateTime,createdBy"
        ),
        "$orderby": "lastModifiedDateTime desc",
        "$top": str(top),
    }
    if filters:
        params["$filter"] = " and ".join(filters)

    result = sfsf_get("/odata/v2/cust_ContractRenewalCaseV2", params)

    if isinstance(result, dict) and not result.get("error"):
        records = result.get("d", {}).get("results", [])
        if not records:
            return {
                "message": "No contract renewal cases found",
                "filters_applied": {
                    "employee_id": employee_id,
                    "status": status,
                    "department": department,
                    "faculty": faculty,
                },
            }

    return result

Key Architectural Highlights & Considerations

Proxy Client Credentials: The clientId and clientSecret parameters correspond to the IAS proxy application (A2A_Proxy_App), not the custom agent itself. This destination handles the token assertion request sent to the custom agent. Joule automatically manages the initial authentication flow before resolving this destination.

Dependency Mapping (tokenService.body.resource): This property targets the IAS dependency name. The prefix urn:sap:identity:application:provider:name: must be prepended to the exact target application dependency configured in IAS (e.g., proxy-to-target).

User Token Validation (x_user_token.jwks_uri): This parameter points to the JWKS endpoint of your IAS tenant, enabling the SAP BTP Destination Service to cryptographically validate the inbound end-user token before issuing the downstream assertion. Warning: Omitting x_user_token.jwks_uri causes the Destination Service to fail user token validation and silently fall back to a technical service user, breaking end-to-end principal propagation.

App-to-App Mode (apptoapp=true): Explicitly enables App2App authentication mode within the SAP BTP Destination Service.
